To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the gut immune system has evolved to support T reg cell neo-conversion via retinoic-acid-producing lamina propria DCs.
the small intestine lamina propia dendritic cells promote the de novo generation of regulatory T cells via retinoico acid.
small intestine lamina proprial dendritic cells promote T reg cell conversion via TGF-β, retinoic acid, and retinoic-acid–induced TGF-β.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that control the development of Foxp3+ regulatory T (Treg) cells.
the role of vitamin A in regulating the immune response in the gastrointestinal tract.
the development and function of regulatory T cells (Tregs) in the gut.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the small intestinal lamina propria contains an environment that promotes de novo generation of regulatory T cells.
the gut environment supports extrathymically induced T reg cell conversion via a mechanism that is dependent on TGFβ and RA, both of which are highly expressed in the gut.
the gut environment supports the development of Treg cells through the production of RA by LpDC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the small intestine has a unique environment that supports the generation of regulatory T ( T reg ) cells from naïve T cells.
the small intestine is the major site for de novo T reg cell generation and this process is facilitated by the gut environment, especially by the LpDCs.
LpDCs promote de novo generation (conversion) of Treg cells via retinoac acid.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gut is a privileged site for T reg cell generation.
the gut environment promotes the development of Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (T reg cells) in the periphery.
the small intestine lamina propia (Lp) is an important site for the peripheral generation of Foxp-3+ T reg cells.
